title: Financing to buy a business
metaDescription: Buying a business often starts with acquisition financing, SBA 7(a), and conventional term-loan comparisons. Learn which routes commonly fit the deal you are evaluating.
summary: The buy-a-business use-case page compares the most common financing starting points when the goal is purchasing an established business or buying out a partner.

hero.title: Buying a business? Start with the financing paths built for the deal.
hero.lead: The right starting point depends on the target business, the purchase structure, and whether the transaction needs working capital alongside the acquisition. This page compares the paths borrowers most often review first.

quickAnswer.definition: usually starts with acquisition-focused financing, SBA 7(a), or conventional term debt, depending on the target company, purchase structure, and whether the request also includes working capital or transition costs.

bestFitProducts.title: Business acquisition financing
bestFitProducts.description: Start here when the request is centered on purchasing an operating business, buying out a partner, or funding an ownership transition.

bestFitProducts.title: SBA 7(a) loans
bestFitProducts.description: SBA 7(a) is often part of the comparison when the deal includes goodwill, working capital, or a broader use of funds than the purchase itself.

bestFitProducts.title: Business term loans
bestFitProducts.description: Conventional term debt can be worth comparing when the target business cash flow supports a fixed repayment structure.

whoItFits.heading: When buying-a-business financing tends to fit
items: Buying an established, cash-flowing business rather than starting from scratch
Buying out a partner or shareholder with a defined transition plan
Evaluating SBA-backed and conventional debt side by side before choosing a structure
Transactions where the purchase terms, target financials, and use of funds can already be documented

whenItMayNotFit.heading: When this path may not fit as well
items: If there is no target business, letter of intent, or clear purchase structure yet, the deal usually needs more definition before financing comparisons become useful.
If the real need is short-term operating cash rather than an acquisition, working-capital routes are usually the better first comparison.

typicalDocuments.heading: Common document examples for buying a business
items: Purchase agreement or letter of intent
Personal financial information from the buyer
Use-of-funds summary showing the transaction structure

commonQuestions.question: What financing paths are commonly compared when buying a business?
commonQuestions.answer: Borrowers often start with acquisition financing, SBA 7(a), and conventional term debt, depending on the deal structure and whether the request also includes working capital or transition costs.

commonQuestions.question: Can SBA 7(a) be used to buy a business?
commonQuestions.answer: Yes. SBA 7(a) is commonly used for business acquisitions and partner buyouts, subject to SBA rules and lender underwriting.

commonQuestions.question: What documents usually matter most for a business purchase?
commonQuestions.answer: Common examples include the target business’s financial statements, the purchase agreement or letter of intent, personal financial information from the buyer, and a clear use-of-funds summary. Exact requirements vary by lender and by transaction.

commonQuestions.question: Does Fund44 finance the acquisition directly?
commonQuestions.answer: No. Fund44 does not finance business purchases directly. Lenders decide eligibility, structure, and terms.
